extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and mathematics-education researchers interested in explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria for when mathematical arguments (proofs or non-proofs) count as explanations: what features make a proof explanatory, when a non-proof can explain, and what anti-patterns fail to explain. Focuses on salience, generalizability, and tracing differences that block proof-extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner's generalizability criterion for explanatory proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof explains a theorem concerning a class S1 iff the proof reveals how the theorem depends on S1's 'characterizing property' — concretely, the proof's 'proof idea' is generalizable: replacing S1's characterizing property by that of another class S2 yields a deformation of the proof that proves an analogous theorem for S2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Steiner (1978): explanatory power is tied to a proof's ability to generalize (via a retained proof idea) to prove analogous theorems for other classes in the same 'family'. This is an orthodox account the paper examines and builds from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience requirement for explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether something requires an explanation (and what would count as one) depends on a salient feature of the explanandum; if a result has no especially striking feature, then there's nothing beyond a proof that it would be to explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The calculator-number theorem is salient because it reveals a common feature (divisibility by 37); the question about an integral equalling 4 (without context) may have no 'why' beyond proof. Context that highlights contrast (e.g., finite vs infinite cases) makes a why-question well-posed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory proofs must exploit a feature of the setup
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof explains when it derives the theorem's salient feature by exploiting another feature of the setup that all cases share (e.g., the proof traces common divisibility back to a shared algebraic representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculator-number example: explanatory proof traces divisibility-by-37 to the representation 105a + 104(a+d)+…; brute-force checking is non-explanatory because it identifies no common origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-proof explanation by tracing salient difference
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory non-proof explains a theorem (e.g., failure of a rule in the infinite case) by taking the salient difference (often a contrast with another result) and tracing that difference to another respect in which the cases differ—a respect distinct from but required by cardinality or the primary contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: explain why the sum rule fails in the infinite case by showing how the difference from the finite case arises from a further difference (no guarantee of a positive d <= every di). This need not prove the explanandum; it need only show why the contrast occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what blocks generalization (mechanism-identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory (non-)proof should identify what specifically stops a finite-case proof idea from generalizing to the target case (i.e., point to the particular step or assumption that fails), thereby revealing the 'mechanism' by which the difference arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the infinite-sum example the argument shows that the step selecting the smallest of finitely many δ_i fails for infinitely many δ_i; pointing this out is what gives explanatory power. 'Mechanism' here is heuristic: pinpoint the proof step that is derailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitivity of what counts as explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A why-question and its acceptable explanations are context-sensitive: asking 'why' often presupposes a contrast (e.g., comparison to finite cases, or to a standard theorem) and the explanation must address that contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without the contrast to finite cases, 'why does the sum rule fail?' is ill-posed as distinct from 'give a proof'. Textbooks present non-proofs as answering 'What goes wrong with the infinite series?' which supplies the context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-generalizability can be explanatory only if it is the right kind
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's (or proof idea's) failure to generalize can count as an explanation only when the failure is shown to stem from a concrete difference between the compared cases (not merely that the former is finite and the latter infinite), and when that difference is relevant to the salient feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper contrasts two non-generalizability cases: (a) the di-based explanation which identifies a relevant blocking feature (explanatory), and (b) the bootstrapping/induction-style argument which simply cannot reach infinity but identifies no blocking feature (non-explanatory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: 'proof by example' (brute-force counterexample) is non-explanatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibiting a particular example that demonstrates the truth of a theorem (or counterexample that shows failure) often fails to explain why the phenomenon occurs because it doesn't trace the phenomenon to a shared origin or blocking feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., showing a divergent derivative series at x=1/2 proves the sum rule can fail, but does not explain why—in contrast to an argument showing why finite-case proof-step fails in infinite case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: bootstrapping/induction without identifying a blocker
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument that bootstraps from n to n+1 (and thus to all finite n) but that simply lacks potential to reach infinity is non-explanatory because it fails to identify any distinct property of the infinite case responsible for the breakdown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such arguments are non-generalizable, their failure to reach the infinite case is uninformative about why the infinite case differs; they contain no step that goes through in finite cases but is blocked in the infinite case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory sufficiency of non-proofs for the salient contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: When the explanandum's salient feature is a contrast (e.g., finite vs infinite), an explanation need not be a proof of the explanandum; it suffices to show how that contrast arises by derailing a finite-case proof idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence explanatory non-proofs are legitimately explanatory even though they do not prove the theorem being explained; their job is to reveal why a relevant proof approach fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to specify what would avoid the blockage (constructive specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong explanatory non-proof will characterise what an infinite case would have to be like for the finite-case proof to carry over, i.e., specify conditions under which the blocking feature would not arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., note that some infinite sums with uniform convergence avoid the issue (footnote 6); pointing out such conditions helps show the explanatory role of the blocking feature, though such helpfulness is not the source of explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish explanatory power from instrumental helpfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument's usefulness in constructing further counterexamples or guiding discovery is a consequence of its explanatory power, not its source; explanatory status is grounded in tracing relevant differences, not in pragmatic utility alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that being helpful for finding counterexamples may follow from being explanatory, but helpfulness by itself does not make an argument explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations of comparative difficulty identify obstacles to standard strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain why one problem is much harder than a similar one, one should identify the obstacle that prevents a standard proof strategy from generalizing or succeeding — analogous to identifying what blocks a proof from extending to the infinite case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper cites examples (e.g., Riemann zeta values) and suggests that explaining 'why so much harder?' involves tracing the blocking difference that derails the formerly successful strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family/analogy requirement for what counts as relevant generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: For generalizability (or non-generalizability) to be explanatory, the theorems/proofs compared must concern classes that belong to the same 'family' or be sufficiently analogous so that the deformation of the proof idea is meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes that the calculator-number proof doesn't belong to the same family as sums of infinitely many differentiable functions, so its non-generalizability is irrelevant to explaining the sum-rule failure; family-membership (analogy) matters.
